flawed_step: Lines 0009-0013 (the justification that d/dz O(z^{-1}) = O(z^{-1}), resting on the malformed bound on line 0011)
counterexample: The only fact the proof invokes to control the differentiated error term is a magnitude bound on the error term itself (line 0011). That implication is false. Take h(x) = sin(e^x)/x for real x > 1 (real x > 1 lies inside every sector |arg z| < pi - eps, |z| > 1). Then |h(x)| <= 1/x for all x > 1, so h(x) = O(x^{-1}) with implied constant c = 1, exactly the hypothesis the proof states on line 0011. But h'(x) = e^x cos(e^x)/x - sin(e^x)/x^2, and at x_k = ln(2 pi k) (k = 1, 2, ...) we have sin(e^{x_k}) = 0 and cos(e^{x_k}) = 1, so h'(x_k) = 2 pi k / ln(2 pi k). For k = 1000 this is 6283.2/8.7 = 722.6, while x_k^{-1} = 0.115; the ratio |h'(x_k)|/|x_k^{-1}| = 6283 grows without bound as k -> infinity. So h = O(x^{-1}) yet h' is not O(x^{-1}) (indeed h' is not even bounded). Hence 'it follows directly' on line 0013 does not follow from line 0011. Separately, line 0011 as literally written is broken: its bound is c/|z^{-1}| = c|z|, an upper bound that GROWS linearly, and the left half '-c/|z^{-1}| < |O(z^{-1})|' is vacuous since the middle quantity is an absolute value; e.g. at z = 100 it asserts only |O(z^{-1})| < 100c, which is compatible with the error term being as large as 99c, not O(z^{-1}) at all.
reasoning_summary: The differentiation of the Stirling expansion in lines 0003-0007 is algebraically correct (d/dz[(z-1/2)ln z - z] = ln z - 1/(2z)). The proof's single substantive gap is the treatment of the derivative of the error term. To conclude that d/dz O(z^{-1}) is again O(z^{-1}) one needs analyticity plus a Cauchy estimate on a slightly shrunken sector (which would give O(z^{-2})); the proof instead offers only a pointwise magnitude bound on the error term (line 0011) and asserts the conclusion 'directly'. A pointwise size bound on a function never controls its derivative: sin(e^x)/x is bounded by 1/x on x > 1 while its derivative is unbounded, blowing up like 2 pi k/ln(2 pi k) at x = ln(2 pi k). Moreover the inequality on line 0011 is itself written with the reciprocal inverted (c/|z^{-1}| = c|z|), so even as a bound on the error term it is far too weak to say anything, and its lower-bound half is vacuous. The theorem statement is true, but the proof as written does not establish it.
counterexample_target: the inference 'error term is O(z^{-1}) => its derivative is O(z^{-1})' used at line 0013
